summary: Shows that at high data rates, the 16-bit IP identification field is too small to avoid frequently mixing up fragments, and TCP and UDP checksums may not catch the resulting corrupted data. It describes experiments demonstrating the problem and discusses operational implications. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv4 uses an identification number to put fragments back into datagrams. At high data rates, that number can repeat while old fragments remain, so pieces from different datagrams may be combined.

questions: ipv4 fragmentation problems at high speed
why is the ip id field too small
how does ip id wrap cause data corruption
subtitle: How IPv4 fragments can be paired incorrectly when the identification field wraps

tldr.problem: IPv4 uses a 16-bit identification field to match fragments, and it can be reused before old fragments leave a receiver's buffer.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4963 explains how fragments from different datagrams can be joined and why 16-bit TCP and UDP checksums may not catch every corrupted result.
tldr.outcome: The note recommends avoiding fragmentation where possible or using stronger integrity checks when fragmentation cannot be avoided.

facts.label: Test data corruptions
facts.value: 121 in approximately 10 TB of random data

today: RFC 4963 is an Informational note published in July 2007. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The IPv4 Identification Field
sections.content:
When an IPv4 datagram is fragmented, a receiver matches its pieces using the source address, destination address, protocol, and identification field. The field is 16 bits, so its values can be reused after 65,536 datagrams.

If a sender reuses an identifier before earlier fragments have expired from the receiver's reassembly buffer, fragments from different datagrams may be joined. RFC 4963 examines this risk at modern data rates.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 needs to recognize which fragments belong together. Its 16-bit identifier can repeat while fragments from an earlier datagram are still waiting.

sections.title: Corruption and Transport Checksums
sections.content:
A receiver may deliver a mis-associated datagram if its transport checksum does not detect the error. TCP and UDP checksums are 16 bits, so the RFC says some incorrectly assembled datagrams can pass the check.

The authors tested fragmented UDP transfers using 1524-byte datagrams over a 1500-byte MTU. In approximately 10 TB of random test data, they observed 121 data corruptions caused by mis-associated fragments.
sections.plainLanguage: A checksum catches many damaged datagrams, but it cannot catch every wrong combination of fragments. The RFC reports that some test corruptions passed the UDP checksum.

sections.title: Preventing or Limiting Mis-Association
sections.content:
The most direct way to avoid this problem is to avoid fragmentation, for example by using Path MTU Discovery. A shorter reassembly timeout may help, but it must also allow slower senders enough time to deliver all fragments.

Tunnels that fragment packets can face the same issue, including when their payload carries TCP traffic. When prevention is impractical, stronger integrity checks above IP can prevent corrupted data from reaching an application, although they do not remove the performance cost of packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: Avoiding fragmentation prevents this kind of fragment mix-up. If a system must fragment packets, stronger integrity checks can help reject corrupted data.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker who knows that two hosts use fragmented IPv4 traffic may send forged fragments with a matching source, destination, and protocol. The attacker does not need to know transport ports or sequence numbers to try to corrupt the datagram.

The RFC says IPv4 fragmentation may be unsuitable for critical applications. It advises applications and devices that fragment at high rates to account for the risk and use strong integrity protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A forged fragment can interfere with a fragmented IPv4 flow if it matches the information used to reassemble packets. Critical data should use stronger integrity protection.
